A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, figures, equations and complete appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched despite substantial reorganization and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original RF regression experiments on synthetic data and California Housing, including prediction comparisons, variance measurements and numerical-stability analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original RF experiments and adds trained neural-network comparisons, non-Gaussian weight experiments and finite-ensemble analyses.

M1.justification: The RF ridge/minimum-norm regressors and arithmetic averaging procedure remain unchanged. Added neural-network experiments and alternative weight distributions are experimental configurations, rather than a new proposed algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions use synthetic sinusoidal regression and California Housing regression. The neural-network experiments increase sample counts on the existing dataset; alternative feature-weight distributions do not introduce new data populations or tasks.

E2.justification: v2 adds single trained three-layer MLPs as comparators for neural-network ensembles in Figures 2, 3 and 17. The existing RF, kernel-regressor and GP-variance comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New neural-network experiments use 12,000 training, 3,000 validation and 5,000 test samples, 1,000 training epochs and validation-selected checkpoints (Appendix B.1). Additional RF experiments introduce Uniform(-10, 10) and Laplace(0, 1) weights and ensemble sizes M = 5, 10, 20 and 40. Existing RF protocols are largely retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds checks of dependence on the feature-weight distribution, finite-ensemble convergence, and neural-network residual alignment (Figures 10, 11, 13 and 17). These substantially extend tests of the theory's applicability. Existing numerical-instability and GP-variance analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v2 introduces explicitly identified standard-deviation bands for neural-network results in Figures 2 and 3. It does not specify the corresponding repeated-run counts. Existing RF Monte Carlo sample counts remain unchanged.

E6.justification: v2 adds neural-network prediction-gap and generalization curves, non-Gaussian RF outcomes and finite-ensemble convergence results. Figure 17 reports residual correlations increasing from 0.918 at component width 20 to 0.965 at width 110. Most existing RF results remain, but the synthetic-ReLU width sweep and ReLU variance-scaling panels in v1 Figures 3 and 5 are removed.

T1.justification: v2 adds the non-asymptotic Theorem 3.3 and Appendix C.2, including kernel-operator definitions, stronger Assumption C.3 and Theorem C.4 with its concentration-based proof. This addresses finite ensembles versus a single RF model using the same features; v1 relied on variance-scaling arguments. Earlier limiting-equivalence, ridge-continuity and underparameterized results are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions and conclusion add a central claim of rapid finite-budget functional convergence supported by a new high-probability theorem. v1's finite-budget contribution concerned similar variance and generalization scaling. The infinite-limit equivalence and interpretation of ensemble variance remain central claims.

C2.justification: Appendix B.2 newly discusses a neural-network discrepancy: independently trained ensembles are more mutually consistent than large single models, contrary to the RF expectations. It proposes training instability as an untested explanation. v1's general concluding limitations paragraph is removed, while RF numerical caveats remain in Appendix A.2.

D1.justification: Appendix B.1 documents the new MLP architecture, SGD training, learning rate 0.01, momentum 0.9 and checkpoint selection. New RF checks specify their weight distributions. Existing RF implementation details, numerical-stability measures and code-access information remain substantially unchanged.

R1.justification: Related work gains a dedicated deep-ensemble discussion and substantive comparisons with Hao et al. and concurrent Ruben et al. Additional Gaussian-universality literature clarifies when those approximations are appropriate. The revision more explicitly positions its non-Gaussian, finite-budget and small-ridge analyses relative to prior research.

P1.justification: The introduction and contributions are extensively rewritten, three guiding questions become two, and finite-budget analysis receives its own subsection before uncertainty quantification. Main-text proof sketches are removed while appendix proofs remain, and a separate neural-network appendix reorganizes the supplementary material.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figures 2 and 3 combine retained RF panels with new neural-network panels, the earlier residual histogram moves to Appendix Figure 12, and new distributional, ensemble-size and residual-correlation figures substantially expand the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: The new MLP experiments, distributional checks, uncertainty bands and training details strengthen empirical grounding beyond v1's RF-only experiments. However, the new rapid finite-budget convergence claim exceeds what the displayed Theorem 3.3/C.4 bound establishes: its confidence-dependent additive term does not shrink with width. Appendix B.2 also identifies an unresolved neural/RF variance discrepancy. These empirical gains and limitations of the strengthened central claim prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.
